name: Charles Francis Richardson
bio: Charles Francis Richardson (1851–1913) was an American critic and poet, born at Hallowell, Maine. He graduated at Dartmouth College, where he became professor of English literature in 1882, having served on the staff of the Independent from 1872 to 1878.

His books include a Primer of American Literature (1878), the verse collection The Cross (1879) and a two-volume History of American Literature (1887–89). Stedman included three of his poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poems.title: Prayer
poems.author: Charles Francis Richardson
poems.collection: An American Anthology, 1787–1900, ed. Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900)
poems.text:
If, when I kneel to pray,
    With eager lips I say:
“Lord, give me all the things that I desire,—
Health, wealth, fame, friends, brave heart, religious fire,
The power to sway my fellow-men at will,
And strength for mighty works to banish ill,”—
    In such a prayer as this
    The blessing I must miss.

    Or if I only dare
    To raise this fainting prayer:
“Thou seest, Lord, that I am poor and weak,
And cannot tell what things I ought to seek;
I therefore do not ask at all, but still
I trust thy bounty all my wants to fill,”—
    My lips shall thus grow dumb,
    The blessing shall not come.

    But if I lowly fall,
    And thus in faith I call:
“Through Christ, O Lord, I pray thee give to me
Not what I would, but what seems best to thee
Of life, of health, of service, and of strength,
Until to thy full joy I come at length,”—
    My prayer shall then avail,
    The blessing shall not fail.

poems.title: After Death
poems.author: Charles Francis Richardson
poems.collection: An American Anthology, 1787–1900, ed. Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900)
poems.text:
When I forth fare beyond this narrow earth,
With all its metes and bounds of now and here,
And brooding clouds of ignorance and fear
That overhung me on my day of birth,
Wherethrough the jocund sun’s perennial mirth
Has shone more inly bright each coming year
With some new glory of that outer sphere
Where length and breadth and height are little worth,
Then shall I find that even here below
We guessed the secret of eternity,
And learned in years the yearless mystery;
For in our earliest world we came to know
The master-lesson and the riddle’s key:
Unending love unending growth shall be.

poems.title: A Conjecture
poems.author: Charles Francis Richardson
poems.collection: An American Anthology, 1787–1900, ed. Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900)
poems.text:
I wonder, dear, if you had been
  The maiden queen’s pet maid of honor,
A flower of that fair time wherein
  A court of roses smiled upon her,

And I, erewhile, by Trojan wall
  Had fiercely fought for Grecian glory,
Beheld the pride of Priam fall,
  And home in Athens told the story,

Whether we, wandering in the glow
  Of the Hereafter’s radiant spaces,
Would there have mutely met, and so
  Seen love make bright our yearning faces.
